title: SQL for Data Analytics
description: Fresher-focused SQL concepts, examples, analytics patterns, practice and interview preparation.

blocks.text:
SELECT
Definition: SELECT tells SQL which columns or calculated expressions you want in the result.
Why use it? Every analytical query starts by deciding what information the business user needs to see.
Benefit: It prevents unnecessary columns from being returned and makes the result easier to read.
Example:

Why use it? Useful for exploring an unfamiliar table during development.
Benefit: Fast inspection, but avoid it in production queries when you only need a few columns.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP;
Calculated columns
Definition: SQL can calculate a new value from existing columns.

Why use it? Analytics often needs derived measures such as annual salary, margin or variance.
Benefit: You can answer business questions without physically adding a new column to the table.
Example:

SELECT ENAME, SAL, SAL * 12 AS ANNUAL_SAL FROM EMP;
3. WHERE — filtering rows
WHERE
Definition: WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation.
Why use it? Most real analytics questions contain a condition: employees earning above a threshold, completed orders, a particular region,
and so on.

Benefit: Reduces the data you process and focuses the answer on the required records.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE SAL > 2000;

Operator
Meaning
Example

JOB <> 'CLERK'

4. Logical operators
AND

Definition: AND requires all conditions to be true.
Why use it? Use it when the business rule has multiple requirements.
Benefit: Creates precise filters.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE JOB = 'CLERK' AND SAL < 1500;
OR

Definition: OR requires at least one condition to be true.
Why use it? Use it when multiple alternatives are acceptable.
Benefit: Useful for category or region alternatives.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO = 10 OR JOB = 'ANALYST';

NOT
Definition: NOT reverses a condition.
Why use it? Use it to exclude a condition.
Benefit: Makes exclusion logic explicit.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE NOT JOB = 'MANAGER';

IN
Definition: IN checks whether a value belongs to a list.
Why use it? It is cleaner than writing many OR conditions.
Benefit: Makes multi-value filters readable.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO IN (10, 20, 30);
NOT IN
Definition: NOT IN excludes values from a list.

Why use it? Useful when you want everything except selected categories.
Benefit: Readable exclusion filter.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO NOT IN (10, 30);

BETWEEN
Definition: BETWEEN checks whether a value falls within an inclusive range.
Why use it? Useful for salary bands, dates and numeric ranges.
Benefit: Shorter and easier to read than two comparisons.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE SAL BETWEEN 1000 AND 3000;

5. LIKE — searching text patterns
LIKE
Definition: LIKE matches text against a pattern. In common SQL syntax, % means any number of characters and _ means one
character.
Why use it? Names, product codes, emails and descriptions rarely have exact values. Pattern matching lets you find partial matches.
Benefit: Powerful for data exploration and text-based filtering.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE ENAME LIKE 'A%';

Pattern
Meaning
Example

Starts with A
ADAMS

Ends with S
JONES

Pattern
Meaning

6. NULL — missing/unknown values
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Definition: NULL represents missing or unknown information; it is not the same as zero or an empty string.
Why use it? Analytics datasets often contain missing commissions, dates, addresses or measurements.
Benefit: Correct NULL handling prevents wrong counts and comparisons.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL, COMM FROM EMP WHERE COMM IS NOT NULL;
Never write COMM = NULL. SQL uses IS NULL and IS NOT NULL for NULL checks.

7. Aggregate functions — turning rows into numbers
COUNT
Definition: COUNT returns a count of rows or non-null values.
Why use it? Use it for record counts, customers, orders and employees.
Benefit: Essential for KPIs and data-quality checks.
Example:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS EMP_COUNT FROM EMP;

SUM
Definition: SUM adds numeric values.
Why use it? Use it for revenue, salary cost, quantity and other totals.
Benefit: Creates core financial and operational KPIs.
Example:
SELECT SUM(SAL) AS TOTAL_SALARY FROM EMP;

AVG
Definition: AVG returns the arithmetic mean.
Why use it? Use it to understand typical salary, revenue or order value.
Benefit: Provides a central tendency measure.
Example:
SELECT AVG(SAL) AS AVG_SALARY FROM EMP;

MIN / MAX
Definition: MIN returns the smallest value; MAX returns the largest.
Why use it? Useful for ranges, highest salary, earliest date and latest date.
Benefit: Quickly identifies boundaries and extremes.
Example:

SELECT MIN(SAL) AS MIN_SAL, MAX(SAL) AS MAX_SAL FROM EMP;
8. GROUP BY — summarizing by category
GROUP BY
Definition: GROUP BY combines rows that share the same grouping value so aggregate functions can calculate one result per

group.
Why use it? Business questions usually ask for metrics by department, job, region, month or product.
Benefit: It turns raw rows into management-level summaries.
Example:

SELECT DEPTNO, COUNT(*) AS EMP_COUNT, AVG(SAL) AS AVG_SALARY FROM EMP GROUP BY DEPTNO;
Rule: if you SELECT a normal column together with an aggregate, that normal column generally belongs in GROUP BY (unless the SQL

dialect/query structure makes it functionally dependent).
9. HAVING — filtering groups

HAVING
Definition: HAVING filters grouped results after GROUP BY.
Why use it? WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.
Benefit: Lets you answer questions such as 'which departments have more than 3 employees?'
Example:
SELECT DEPTNO, COUNT(*) AS EMP_COUNT FROM EMP GROUP BY DEPTNO HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;

Use
Correct clause
Example
Filter individual rows

WHERE
WHERE SAL > 2000
Filter grouped results

HAVING
HAVING AVG(SAL) > 2000
10. ORDER BY — sorting results
ORDER BY

Definition: ORDER BY sorts the final result by one or more columns or expressions.
Why use it? Analytics outputs often need highest-to-lowest, newest-to-oldest or alphabetical ordering.
Benefit: Makes reports and ranking queries understandable.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL FROM EMP ORDER BY SAL DESC;

ASC = ascending. DESC = descending. If direction is omitted, ascending is usually assumed.

13. Subqueries — SQL inside SQL
Single-row subquery
Definition: A subquery is a query nested inside another query. A single-row subquery returns one value.
Why use it? Useful when a condition depends on a value calculated or found by another query.
Benefit: Lets you express comparisons such as 'employees earning more than KING'.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL FROM EMP WHERE SAL > ( SELECT SAL FROM EMP WHERE ENAME = 'KING' );

Same department as another employee
Definition: A subquery can first find a department number and the outer query can use it.
Why use it? Useful for relationship-based questions without manually looking up IDs.
Benefit: Makes dynamic comparisons possible.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, DEPTNO FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO = ( SELECT DEPTNO FROM EMP WHERE ENAME = 'JONES' );
Annual salary comparison
Definition: You can compare a calculated expression against a calculated value from a subquery.

Why use it? Useful when the business metric is not stored directly.
Benefit: Keeps calculations close to the question.
Example:
SELECT EMPNO, ENAME, SAL * 12 AS ANNUAL_SAL FROM EMP WHERE SAL * 12 > ( SELECT SAL * 12 FROM EMP WHERE ENAME = 'WARD' );

14. Multi-row subqueries: IN, ANY and ALL
IN with a subquery
Definition: IN checks whether a value exists in a set returned by a subquery.
Why use it? Use when the inner query can return multiple values.
Benefit: Natural for category membership across tables.
Example:
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO IN ( SELECT DEPTNO FROM DEPT WHERE DNAME IN ('ACCOUNTING','SALES') );

ALL
Definition: ALL requires a comparison to be true against every value returned by the subquery.
Why use it? Use for conditions such as greater than every salesperson salary.
Benefit: Expresses strict comparison against an entire set.
Example:
SELECT ENAME FROM EMP WHERE SAL > ALL ( SELECT SAL FROM EMP WHERE JOB = 'SALESMAN' );

ANY
Definition: ANY requires a comparison to be true against at least one value returned by the subquery.
Why use it? Use for comparisons against any member of a set.
Benefit: Useful for flexible multi-row comparisons.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL FROM EMP WHERE SAL < ANY ( SELECT SAL FROM EMP WHERE JOB = 'MANAGER' );
15. Nested subqueries

Nested subquery
Definition: A nested query contains one subquery inside another subquery.
Why use it? Useful when the answer depends on multiple levels of lookup.
Benefit: Handles complex relationship and ranking questions.
Example:

SELECT DNAME FROM DEPT WHERE DEPTNO = ( SELECT DEPTNO FROM EMP WHERE SAL = ( SELECT MAX(SAL) FROM EMP WHERE SAL < (
SELECT MAX(SAL) FROM EMP ) ) );

For a fresher, understand the logic first. Don't memorize nested queries character-by-character. Break them into the innermost question, then
work outward.
16. JOIN — combining related tables

INNER JOIN
Definition: An inner join returns rows where the join condition matches in both tables.

Why use it? Real datasets are normalized: employee details and department details often live in different tables.
Benefit: Lets analysts combine dimensions and facts into one useful result.
Example:

SELECT e.ENAME, d.DNAME, d.LOC FROM EMP e JOIN DEPT d ON e.DEPTNO = d.DEPTNO;
Join type

Simple meaning
Typical use
INNER JOIN

Only matching rows
Employees with valid departments
LEFT JOIN

All left rows + matches
Find missing dimension records
RIGHT JOIN

All right rows + matches
Less common; reverse of LEFT
FULL OUTER JOIN
All rows from both sides

Reconciliation / completeness
CROSS JOIN
Every left row paired with every right row
Controlled combinations
SELF JOIN
A table joined to itself
Employee-manager hierarchy
17. Join conditions
The most important idea is the join key. In the source, EMP.DEPTNO connects to DEPT.DEPTNO. The MGR column in EMP points
to another EMP.EMPNO, creating a manager hierarchy.
SELECT e.ENAME, d.DNAME FROM EMP e JOIN DEPT d ON e.DEPTNO = d.DEPTNO WHERE e.JOB = 'SALESMAN';
If you forget the ON condition, you can accidentally create a Cartesian product and multiply rows. That's one of the classic beginner mistakes.

18. SELF JOIN — employee and manager
Self join
Definition: A self join joins a table to itself using different aliases. Your source uses E1, E2 and E3 to represent employee, manager
and manager's manager.

Why use it? Hierarchical data often lives in one table.
Benefit: Lets you answer reporting-chain questions.
Example:
SELECT e1.ENAME AS EMPLOYEE, e2.ENAME AS MANAGER FROM EMP e1 JOIN EMP e2 ON e1.MGR = e2.EMPNO;

Manager's manager
Definition: Join the employee table three times to move two levels up the hierarchy.
Why use it? Useful for organizational reporting and hierarchy analysis.
Benefit: Shows how relational tables can represent tree-like relationships.
Example:

SELECT e1.ENAME AS EMPLOYEE, e2.ENAME AS MANAGER, e3.ENAME AS MANAGER_MANAGER FROM EMP e1 JOIN EMP e2 ON e1.MGR =
e2.EMPNO JOIN EMP e3 ON e2.MGR = e3.EMPNO;

Your source contains many self-join questions: employee + manager, employee + manager's salary, employee + manager + manager's
manager, and combinations with department information.
19. TOP-N and Nth salary problems
Top-N
Definition: Top-N means selecting the highest or lowest N records according to a metric such as salary.
Why use it? Very common in interviews and business analytics.
Benefit: Builds ranking skills and introduces window functions.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL FROM EMP ORDER BY SAL DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY;

Nth highest salary with DENSE_RANK
Definition: DENSE_RANK assigns the same rank to equal values without gaps in the next rank.
Why use it? Useful when duplicate salaries should share a rank.
Benefit: Handles ties more naturally than simple row numbering.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, SAL FROM ( SELECT ENAME, SAL, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SAL DESC) AS rnk FROM EMP ) WHERE rnk = 3;

Nth highest salary with a distinct-count idea
Definition: The source also demonstrates a classic correlated-subquery technique using COUNT(DISTINCT salary) to find the Nth
distinct salary.
Why use it? Useful for understanding ranking without window functions.
Benefit: Builds strong SQL reasoning, although window functions are usually clearer in modern SQL.
Example:
SELECT e1.SAL FROM EMP e1 WHERE 2 = ( SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.SAL) FROM EMP e2 WHERE e2.SAL > e1.SAL );

20. Window functions — the most important advanced
analytics skill
Window function
Definition: A window function calculates across related rows while keeping the original row-level detail.
Why use it? GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; window functions let you calculate rankings, running totals and comparisons without

losing individual rows.
Benefit: Extremely useful for real-world analytics, reporting and interview problems.
Example:
SELECT ENAME, DEPTNO, SAL, AVG(SAL) OVER (PARTITION BY DEPTNO) AS DEPT_AVG FROM EMP;

Function
What it does
Common use
ROW_NUMBER()
Unique sequential number
Top N without ties
RANK()
Same rank for ties, gaps after ties
Competition ranking
DENSE_RANK()
Same rank for ties, no gaps
Nth distinct value
LAG()
Looks at previous row
Previous month/value
LEAD()
Looks at next row
Next event/value
SUM() OVER

Running/windowed total
Cumulative revenue
AVG() OVER

Windowed average
Average by department
21. ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
Salary
ROW_NUMBER
RANK
DENSE_RANK
Think: ROW_NUMBER = every row gets a different number. RANK = ties share rank and create gaps. DENSE_RANK = ties share rank but no
gaps.

22. PARTITION BY
PARTITION BY
Definition: PARTITION BY splits the rows into independent windows before the window function runs.

Why use it? Use it when you need a ranking or metric separately for each department, region, customer or product.
Benefit: Enables questions such as 'top 3 employees in each department'.
Example:

23. LAG and LEAD
LAG

Definition: LAG reads a value from a previous row in the window order.
Why use it? Use it for month-over-month comparisons, previous transactions and changes.

Benefit: Turns row-level data into time-series comparisons.
Example:
SELECT OrderDate, Revenue, LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS PREV_REVENUE FROM Sales;
LEAD
Definition: LEAD reads a value from a following row.

Why use it? Useful for next-event dates, future values and intervals.
Benefit: Helps calculate time until the next event.
Example:

SELECT CustomerID, OrderDate, LEAD(OrderDate) OVER ( PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate ) AS NEXT_ORDER FROM
Orders;

24. CTE — Common Table Expression
CTE
Definition: A CTE is a named temporary result defined with WITH and used by the query that follows it.
Why use it? Complex queries become much easier to read when you break them into logical stages.
Benefit: Improves readability, debugging and reuse within a single statement.
Example:
WITH high_salary AS ( SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE SAL > 1000 ) SELECT * FROM high_salary;

CTE + aggregation
Definition: A CTE can calculate an intermediate summary that another query consumes.
Why use it? Useful for multi-stage analytics.
Benefit: Makes complicated logic easier to reason about.
Example:

WITH dept_stats AS ( SELECT DEPTNO, COUNT(*) AS EMP_COUNT, AVG(SAL) AS AVG_SAL FROM EMP GROUP BY DEPTNO ) SELECT
d.DNAME, s.EMP_COUNT, s.AVG_SAL FROM dept_stats s JOIN DEPT d ON s.DEPTNO = d.DEPTNO;

Your source explicitly contrasts queries written without CTEs and with CTEs, including a high-salary filter and a department employee-count
example.

27. A real Data Analyst example
Suppose a manager asks: “Which departments have more than 2 employees, and what are their average salaries?”
Step 1 — Identify columns: DEPTNO, COUNT(*), AVG(SAL).
Step 2 — Group: GROUP BY DEPTNO.
Step 3 — Filter groups: HAVING COUNT(*) > 2.

SELECT DEPTNO, COUNT(*) AS EMP_COUNT, AVG(SAL) AS AVG_SALARY FROM EMP GROUP BY DEPTNO HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 ORDER BY
AVG_SALARY DESC;

This is the thinking pattern you should practice: business question → required columns → filters → grouping → calculation → final
presentation.

31. Fresher interview questions
Question
Simple answer
What is SQL?
A language used to query and manipulate data in relational databases.

WHERE vs HAVING?
WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
WHERE vs ON?
ON defines how joined rows match; WHERE filters the resulting rows.
INNER JOIN?
Returns matching rows from both tables.
LEFT JOIN?
Returns all rows from the left table plus matching right-side rows.
GROUP BY?

Creates groups so aggregate functions can calculate one result per group.
Subquery?
A query nested inside another query.
CTE?
A named temporary query result created with WITH.
Window function?
Calculates across related rows while preserving row-level detail.
ROW_NUMBER vs RANK?
ROW_NUMBER gives unique sequence numbers; RANK allows ties and gaps.
DENSE_RANK?
Allows ties without gaps in rank numbers.
SELF JOIN?
Joining a table to itself, commonly for hierarchies.
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs in that column.
NULL?
Missing/unknown value; use IS NULL to test it.

38. Final advice for a fresher
Don't memorize 350 queries. Your uploaded PDF is excellent as a practice bank, but the real goal is to recognize patterns. For
example, many of its questions reduce to a small number of ideas: filtering, grouping, comparing against another row/value, joining
related tables, ranking, hierarchy traversal and staged queries. The source repeatedly exercises those patterns across different
business questions.
Your best sequence is: SELECT → WHERE → operators → aggregate functions → GROUP BY → HAVING → subqueries →

joins → self joins → CTEs → window functions → data-quality checks → business projects.
For Data Analytics, SQL is one of the highest-value skills you can build. For Data Engineering, SQL becomes the foundation for
warehouse work, ETL/ELT, data quality, transformation and performance tuning.
